QnA 1 · What can MAP optimize in this particular attention graph?

There is one opaque attention computation, with ordinary tensor inputs and output. Its internal attention loops remain inside P1. MAP can simplify the surrounding representation, but it has no separate graph-level matmul, softmax or PV producer/consumer pair to fuse here. ↗ fused_attention.py:57 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:82 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:201 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:215

IR1's attention path at MAP entry
  Q ─┐
  K ─┼──► map.iter.opaque ──► O ──► mo.output
  V ─┘       └─ call P1.FusedAttention
                BN=16, BD=8, device=gpu:0

Top-level attention iterator count: 1
Ordinary input roles: Q, K, V
Ordinary output role: O
Scalar attention-body instructions exposed to MAP: none

Identical types do not make %q, %k and %v identical values. All three are used, so operand cleanup cannot merge them simply because each is float32[32,32]. ↗ fused_attention.py:43 ↗ fused_attention.py:61 ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:29

In a one-iterator attention path, there is no second iterator to fuse. The round can inspect candidates and stop with before=1, after=1, fused=0. This is a source-derived expectation for this path, not a measured compiler dump. The source terminates its loop using that exact count comparison. ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:77 ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:84

SOURCE · native definitions behind the branches. The stage builder schedules pass objects on mo.graph, except body outlining which is scheduled at module scope. During pm.run(IR1), the fuser creates and runs its own nested pass managers on each graph. Temporary rewriters, topology analyses, vectors and value maps belong to a pass invocation; the created/moved operations, regions and block arguments remain owned by IR1. Pass-manager execution ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:338 ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:46

Tree branch Concrete native entry and handoff
Elementwise / view / prologue fusion FuseElementwisePass::runOnOperation, FuseViewsPass::runOnOperation and FuseProloguePass::runOnOperation supply different predicates to fuseInput. It visits consumers in reverse topological order within their own blocks.
Reduction fusion FuseReductionsPass::runOnOperation gathers rowwise iterators, repeatedly consumes eligible producers, then eligible consumers.
Epilogue / reshape-epilogue fusion FuseEpiloguePass::runOnOperation and FuseReshapeEpiloguePass::runOnOperation call fuseOutput. It visits producers before consumers and splices consumer arithmetic into the producer's epilogue.
Horizontal fusion fuse constructs a replacement with merged inputs and concatenated output types, retaining separate destinations.
Mutable loads FuseMutableLoads::runOnOperation chooses between rewiring an existing buffer input, adding chains, or merging with existing chains. maybeGetCompatibleKernel rejects cross-block users and an opaque consumer that also takes the mutable buffer.
Accumulation assignIntermediateTensors identifies each epilogue's storage source; a replacement iterator can gain a scratch result.
Contiguous views / outlining raiseViewChain removes eligible pure view iterators. outline wraps remaining structured iterators and moves their bodies.
View motion loopInvariantViewMotionInClosure rewrites load addresses, then erases unused index transforms. A final invariant check permits only store-feeding index transforms to remain.

MapPipelineOptions has one field here: fuseMutableLoadStore, defaulting to true. It gates the extra mutable-load pass; createFuseKernels() is scheduled unconditionally by this builder. The elementwise pass separately defaults its large-operand threshold to 4096 elements and duplication cap to 64. The shared driver applies that cap to duplication of multi-use producers; moving a sole-use producer does not consume the cap. MAP options Elementwise options Duplication guard

After this builder's passes, gcPipelineImpl may add NaN checks, then an optional map-pre-mogg dump. Check injection follows fusion so a check cannot fuse into the kernel being checked. A dump is a scheduled inspection step, not another compilation representation. ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:585 ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:588 ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:568

QnA 4 · What does canonicalization do to operands and captured values?

TEST · repeated input: a MAP body that receives the same SSA value twice can have one incoming slot while its call still uses that slot twice. This does not change the callee from an Add into a unary operation. ↗ kernel_operands_basic.mlir:20

BEFORE
  map.iter.opaque inputs(%x as %a, %x as %b)
    call Add inputs(%a,%b) outputs(%out)

AFTER
  map.iter.opaque inputs(%x as %a)
    call Add inputs(%a,%a) outputs(%out)

If x[0]=3: Add still receives (3,3) and writes 6.
Outer incoming slots: 2 → 1; call's mathematical inputs: still 2.

For a capturing closure, the implementation identifies duplicate captured Values, redirects uses of duplicate block arguments, then erases those arguments. Dead captures can also be removed. ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:40 ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:56 ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:69

Attention: [%q,%k,%v] → [%q,%k,%v]
Reason: three distinct live SSA values, despite the same shape and dtype.

Eligible duplicate case: [%x,%x] → [%x]
Reason: both slots refer to the very same SSA value.

The repository also checks that deduplicating prologue captures leaves a now-unused load, which the canonicalizer removes. This illustrates why simplifications are applied to a fixed point rather than once per original operation. ↗ kernel_operands_basic.mlir:49

QnA 5 · How does view motion simplify addressing? Use a 2×3 tensor.

TEST · inspected transpose-view example: a per-element index permutation is moved to a strided view outside the loop body. The loop then loads with its own index. The final output store remains. ↗ loop-invariant-view-motion-transpose.mlir:3 ↗ loop-invariant-view-motion-transpose.mlir:16

X = [[0,1,2],
     [3,4,5]]
Shape [2,3], row-major element strides [3,1]

BEFORE · inside each iteration of output shape [3,2]
  input_index = transpose_index([i,j], permutation=[1,0])
  value = load X[input_index]         ← X[j,i]
  store O[i,j] = value

AFTER
  XT = strided_view(X, shape=[3,2], strides=[1,3])
  inside the loop:
    value = load XT[i,j]
    store O[i,j] = value

At output [2,1]: input [1,2]
  offset = 1*3 + 2*1 = 5 elements = 20 bytes for float32
  strided-view offset = 2*1 + 1*3 = 5 elements
  value = 5 in either representation

The hoisted view is an addressing description; it does not require copying the input into a separate transposed allocation. The pass removes repeated index transformation work where the source pattern permits it. Its actual IR uses map.index.transpose.stride. ↗ loop-invariant-view-motion-transpose.mlir:20 ↗ loop-invariant-view-motion-transpose.mlir:25

For attention, Kᵀ is part of the authored kernel computation. This MAP view example does not imply that a graph-level K transpose exists or gets hoisted for FusedAttention. ↗ fused_attention.py:61 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:346

└─ map.iter.opaque

QnA 7 · How do MAP fusion and access optimizations change concrete operations, block arguments, captures and storage requirements? Show worked attention, elementwise, prologue, epilogue, canonicalization, accumulation, view and outlining examples, with native rewrites, numerical checks, matching conditions and skipped cases.

SOURCE / TEST · ten worked examples. The before/after IR is schematic, with short tensor types and symbol names. Each test description identifies whether its input is MO, structured MAP, or already outlined MAP, then names the RUN passes and the relevant expected output. Example 1 · What does the complete MAP stage do to the single opaque attention call?

SOURCE · actual attention route. Assume the live computation is the one custom call from the example, with three distinct Q/K/V values, a single output and BD=8, BN=16. MO→MAP has created ordinary tensor argument paths and no fusion closures. Shape equality does not supply a producer edge, a scalar body, or an identity between Q, K and V. ↗ fused_attention.py:57 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:82 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:201 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:215

BEFORE · MAP entry, schematic; T=f32[32,32] on gpu:0
  graph inputs %q:T, %k:T, %v:T                   // distinct live graph arguments
  %o = map.iter.opaque inputs(%q,%k,%v) outputs(%dst:T) {
    map.call.opaque @PKG.FusedAttention           // P1's registered implementation
      [BD=8, BN=16] inputs(%q,%k,%v) outputs(%dst) // ordinary tensor interfaces
  }
  mo.output %o                                   // only consumer of the output

AFTER · same live computation through buildMapPipeline
  graph inputs %q:T, %k:T, %v:T                   // still distinct graph arguments
  %o = map.iter.opaque inputs(%q,%k,%v) outputs(%dst:T) {
    map.call.opaque @PKG.FusedAttention           // same selected implementation
      [BD=8, BN=16] inputs(%q,%k,%v) outputs(%dst) // same tensor computation
  }
  mo.output %o                                   // same graph result

The fusion driver's termination condition uses the count of outer iterator operations:

unsigned before = kernelCount();
if (failed(runPipeline(fusePm, graphOp)))
  return signalPassFailure();
fused = before - kernelCount();
numKernelsFused += fused;

Its iterator walk returns WalkResult::skip() at each outer iterator, so nested callback iterators are not counted as separate kernel groups. Here the source-derived count is before=1, after=1, fused=0, and the do/while stops after that round. This is a control-flow explanation, not an observed compilation trace. ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:63 ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:77 ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:84

Pass Why the attention computation remains in this form
Input/prologue fusion No elementwise producer or input prologue exists.
Output fusion The attention destination has no epilogue; mo.output is not an elementwise consumer.
Mutable-load fusion This graph fragment has no mo.mutable.load.
Accumulation The pass finds no map.iter.epilogue to assign an intermediate tensor.
Contiguous-view raising There is no structured view iterator to match.
Outlining map.iter.opaque is already the outer kernel form; only structured iterators enter outline.
View motion There is no capturing closure with an index-transform/load chain.
Operand cleanup Q/K/V are distinct and all used.

These outcomes follow from the native candidate selection in findEligibleProducer, findFusibleEdge, accumulation's epilogue walk, outlining's structured worklist, and view motion's closure walk. ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:295

For an illustrative data check, zero Q gives equal attention weights; if every V entry is 2, every output entry remains 2. The stage keeps the same call, inputs and parameters, so it keeps that computation. The next examples use other graph structures that satisfy the transformation predicates. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:90 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:99 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:238

Example 2 · How are an Add producer and Mul consumer spliced into one scalar body?

TEST · MO input, then an isolated MAP subpass. basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir supplies (X+Y)*Z over [8] f32. Its RUN imports kernels, runs --mo-to-map, then --map-fuse-elementwise. The test therefore constructs the two structured MAP iterators before exercising the elementwise fuser; it does not start from hand-authored MAP or run every later MAP optimization. Its checks require one iterator with three inputs, two registered scalar calls, one final store, and provenance from both MO operations. ↗ basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:1 ↗ basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:3 ↗ basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:13

Illustrative X=[2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2], Y=[3,3,3,3,3,3,3,3], Z=[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4]

BEFORE · schematic MAP after MO→MAP
  %t = iterator inputs(X,Y) output(T) index(i) {    // producer, shape [8]
    x = map.load X[i]                              // first scalar operand
    y = map.load Y[i]                              // second scalar operand
    t = map.call.elementwise Add(i,x,y)            // t=5
    map.store T[i] = t                             // materialized intermediate edge
  }
  %o = iterator inputs(%t,Z) output(O) index(j) {   // consumer, shape [8]
    t = map.load T[j]                              // read producer tensor
    z = map.load Z[j]                              // other consumer operand
    o = map.call.elementwise Mul(j,t,z)            // o=20
    map.store O[j] = o                             // final store
  }
  mo.output %o                                    // all eight values are 20

AFTER
  %o = iterator inputs(X,Y,Z) output(O) index(j) {  // one replacement computation group
    x = map.load X[j]                              // producer loads mapped to consumer index
    y = map.load Y[j]                              // same element correspondence
    t = map.call.elementwise Add(j,x,y)            // local SSA scalar, t=5
    z = map.load Z[j]                              // consumer's remaining load
    o = map.call.elementwise Mul(j,t,z)            // use t directly, o=20
    map.store O[j] = o                             // final destination retained
  }
  mo.output %o                                    // same tensor values

FuseElementwisePass accepts a pair only when both are elementwise iterators without view transformations. The shared input-fusion driver prefers a sole-use producer, verifies the block/device/chain constraints and finds the consumer load site. The core splice clones the producer region, extracts its stored scalar and removes its former destination:

rewriter.cloneRegionBefore(src.getBody(), dstRegion, dstRegion.begin());
Block &srcClone = dstRegion.front();

StoreOp storeOp = getUniqueStore(srcClone);
Value fusedVal = storeOp.getValue();
rewriter.eraseOp(storeOp);
srcClone.eraseArgument(numSrcInputs);

It then maps the cloned input arguments to the new consumer input slots and the cloned index to the load's index, inlines the block before that load, replaces the load by fusedVal, and removes the obsolete intermediate input slot. Once the producer result is unused, the driver erases its old iterator. Elementwise predicate Eligibility Splice and rewiring Producer deletion

Changed structure Result
Consumer inputs (T,Z) (X,Y,Z)
Producer store and consumer load of T Removed; their value connection becomes scalar SSA
Top-level iterators 2 → 1
External graph inputs/output Unchanged
Fusion metadata Records Add and Mul ancestry

The intermediate represents eight f32 writes and eight reads, or 8×4×2=64 bytes of illustrative tensor traffic removed from this representation. This excludes all X/Y/Z/O accesses and is not a measured bandwidth figure. ↗ basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:17 ↗ basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:23

Same-index sharing: the file's @fusion_diamond reads one Add result through Mul(t,t) and ReLU(t). At a lane with X=2,Y=3, t=5, so t*t+ReLU(t)=30. The expected body computes Add once. mergeRedundantLoads keys loads by (block,index) before cloning so three same-index reads share one scalar producer computation. ↗ basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:55 ↗ basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:71 Load sharing implementation

Skipped case: this elementwise wrapper rejects a view-bearing producer or consumer; FuseViews has a separate predicate. The shared driver also refuses to move a producer across a block boundary or past a prohibited reshape read. Pure-elementwise predicate Block and reshape guards

Example 3 · Why can a fan-out Add stay separate under one option value and be copied into both consumers under another?

TEST · the elementwise subpass's cost guard. large_operand_dup.mlir runs import → MO→MAP → map-fuse-elementwise twice. The first RUN uses the default threshold; the second sets large-tensor-element-threshold=16384 and checks HIGHTHRESH expectations. Both consume the same graph with two GPU inputs [4096,2], an Add, and two consumers, Tanh and ReLU. Each input has 8192 elements. Both RUN commands Input graph

BEFORE · schematic, all tensors f32[4096,2] on gpu:0
  T = iterator Add(X,Y)                       // one producer with two users
  U = iterator Tanh(T)                        // first consumer
  V = iterator ReLU(T)                        // second consumer
  mo.output U,V                              // both results escape

AFTER default threshold=4096 · duplication skipped
  T = iterator Add(X,Y)                       // two 8192-element inputs count as large
  U = iterator Tanh(T)                        // reads materialized T
  V = iterator ReLU(T)                        // also reads T
  mo.output U,V                              // producer remains shared

AFTER threshold=16384 · duplication matched
  U = iterator { t=Add(X[i],Y[i]); store U[i]=Tanh(t) } // Add copied into first body
  V = iterator { t=Add(X[i],Y[i]); store V[i]=ReLU(t) } // Add copied into second body
  mo.output U,V                              // materialized T no longer needed

The decisive implementation counts expensive input tensors:

std::optional<int64_t> numElements = tensorType.getNumElements();
return !numElements.has_value() || *numElements > largeTensorElementThreshold;

isCheapToDuplicate returns false after the second large input, and config.canDuplicate additionally rejects host kernels. With threshold 4096, both 8192-element inputs are large; with 16384, neither is large. The decision is about additional input reads caused by copying a producer's computation into multiple consumers. Size classification Large-input count Host guard

For illustrative values X[i]=-1, Y[i]=1, each version computes T[i]=0, U[i]=tanh(0)=0 and V[i]=ReLU(0)=0. Input tensor storage is not cloned by the compiler; the duplicated objects are scalar computations inside two kernel bodies. The test's default CHECK requires one Add producer and two readers; HIGHTHRESH requires Add in both consumer bodies. Default expectation Changed-threshold expectation

Another rejection: every user must be able to absorb the duplicated computation. duplicationAllowed rejects a producer whose result also reaches mo.output, because that tensor must still be materialized. The file's @unaryExpEscapingOutput checks that only one Exp remains even though a unary producer has only one large input. All-users guard Escaping-output test

These expected iterator counts stop at the isolated elementwise pass. The full MAP fusion round also has horizontal fusion, which can combine eligible siblings later. A rejection here therefore identifies this particular rewrite decision. ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:47 ↗ FuseKernels.cpp:55

Example 4 · How does gather(Add(A,B), I) compute the Add inside gather's input callback?

TEST · full fusion round after MO lowering. prologue_fusion.mlir imports %kernel_api_test_lib, runs --mo-to-map, then --map-fuse-kernels. In @add_gather, A/B have shape [3,3], I has shape [2,2], and gather's axis-0 output is [2,2,3]. The checks require Add's two loads and scalar call inside gather's data prologue, no standalone elementwise iterator, and operandIndices=[0] in fusion provenance. RUN Input and expectations

Illustrative A=[[0,1,2],[3,4,5],[6,7,8]], B=all 10, I=[[2,0],[1,2]]

BEFORE · schematic MAP
  %t = elementwise Add(A,B)                        // materialize f32[3,3] values 10…18
  %o = opaque inputs(%t,I) outputs(O) {
    %pd = prologue(index d) captures(T) {           // gather's data callback
      v = map.load T[d]                             // read materialized Add result
      map.yield v                                  // scalar value for gather
    }
    %pi = prologue(index k) captures(I) {           // indices callback
      n = map.load I[k]                             // obtain requested row number
      map.yield n                                  // pass row number to gather
    }
    %eo = epilogue(value v,index j) captures(O) {
      map.store O[j] = v                            // gather output destination
    }
    map.call.opaque Gather[axis=0] inputs(%pd,%pi) outputs(%eo) // unchanged gather logic
  }

AFTER
  %o = opaque inputs(I,A,B) outputs(O) {             // old T slot removed, A/B appended
    %pd = prologue(index d) captures(A,B) {           // rebuilt callback dependencies
      a = map.load A[d]                             // producer's first load
      b = map.load B[d]                             // producer's second load
      t = map.call.elementwise Add(d,a,b)           // compute only the requested element
      map.yield t                                  // replace old load result
    }
    %pi = prologue(index k) captures(I) {           // indices callback unchanged
      n = map.load I[k]                             // same selected row
      map.yield n                                  // same row number
    }
    %eo = epilogue(value v,index j) captures(O) {
      map.store O[j] = v                            // same output coordinate
    }
    map.call.opaque Gather[axis=0] inputs(%pd,%pi) outputs(%eo) // use fused data callback
  }
  mo.output %o                                     // [[[16,17,18],[10,11,12]],
                                                   //  [[13,14,15],[16,17,18]]]

findExistingPrologueCapture requires the opaque input argument to have one use in a prologue and the corresponding capture argument to have one load use. This gives the rewriter a precise scalar replacement site. spliceIntoClosure clones the producer body, deletes its store/output argument, appends A/B as opaque inputs and prologue captures, then performs this rewiring:

oldLoad.getResult().replaceAllUsesWith(fusedVal);
oldLoad.erase();
closure.eraseCaptureAt(capture.captureIdx);
dst.eraseInputsAt(argIdx);

The cloned Add receives the old load's index. At output [0,0,2], gather requests data [2,2], so the prologue computes 8+10=18. Before fusion it read the same 18 from T. The opaque body's input slots change from two (T,I) to three (I,A,B); its output destination stays O. The data prologue changes from one captured tensor to two. Capture matcher Native splice Final rewiring

Skipped cases have different causes. @no_fuse_multi_use also returns T, so the prologue fuser's canDuplicate=false and the all-users guard keep the producer. @no_fuse_across_blocks places the producer outside an mo.if branch and its gather inside; the block guard prevents moving it. @no_fuse_plain_input feeds Matmul's ordinary input, for which no prologue load site exists. Each test explicitly checks the surviving elementwise producer. No-duplication policy Multi-use test Block test Plain-input test

The same plain-input limitation applies to the authored attention call's Q/K/V interfaces. This example establishes a gather route with declared callback support. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:83 ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:201

Example 5 · How does Matmul(A,B)+Z become arithmetic in a producer's output callback?

TEST · MO input and the isolated epilogue pass. epilogue_fusion.mlir imports kernels, runs --mo-to-map, then --map-fuse-epilogue. Its @matmul_add supplies [8,8] f32 tensors and checks one opaque iterator whose epilogue loads Z, adds the incoming Matmul scalar and stores the final result. The registered Matmul call still receives A/B and writes through the epilogue. RUN Input and CHECK sequence

Smaller illustrative matrices, all f32[2,2]:
  A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[5,6],[7,8]], Z=[[1,1],[1,1]]
  T=A@B=[[19,22],[43,50]]; O=T+Z=[[20,23],[44,51]]
BEFORE · schematic MAP
  %t = opaque inputs(A,B) outputs(T) {
    %ep = epilogue(value m,index i) captures(T) {    // Matmul's initial output callback
      map.store T[i] = m                            // materialize product element
    }
    map.call.opaque Matmul inputs(A,B) outputs(%ep)  // registered producer
  }
  %o = elementwise inputs(%t,Z) outputs(O) index(i) {
    m = map.load T[i]                               // read product element
    z = map.load Z[i]                               // read added tensor element
    r = map.call.elementwise Add(i,m,z)             // postprocess product
    map.store O[i] = r                              // write final result
  }
  mo.output %o                                     // final graph output

AFTER
  %o = opaque inputs(A,B,Z) outputs(O) {
    %ep = epilogue(value m,index i) captures(O,Z) {  // m arrives directly from Matmul
      z = map.load Z[i]                             // new epilogue capture supplies Z
      r = map.call.elementwise Add(i,m,z)           // same scalar postprocessing
      map.store O[i] = r                            // final destination replaces T
    }
    map.call.opaque Matmul inputs(A,B) outputs(%ep)  // original Matmul implementation
  }
  mo.output %o                                     // same [[20,23],[44,51]]

The epilogue wrapper also checks that the consumer reads the producer at its untransformed loop index. Once matched, fuseOutputOnce replaces every load of the fused input by the scalar already arriving at the epilogue:

for (Operation *user : llvm::to_vector(fusionArg.getUsers())) {
  auto load = cast<LoadOp>(user);
  load.getResult().replaceAllUsesWith(val);
  load.erase();
}

Here val is the Matmul value m, not a new load from T. Other consumer inputs become new opaque inputs and epilogue captures. The old producer store is removed, the consumer body is moved into the epilogue, and a store of finalVal is rebuilt at the destination. Matcher Untransformed-index predicate Load substitution Capture insertion Body move and final stores

For [0,1], Matmul produces 1×6+2×8=22. Before fusion the Add reloads 22; afterward its argument is the incoming scalar 22. It adds Z[0,1]=1 and stores 23 in both forms. The driver redirects the consumer's result users to the producer's revised result and erases the old consumer iterator, while preserving both operations in fusion provenance. Result replacement Provenance and deletion

TEST · input is already MAP. kernel_operands_basic.mlir runs mo-opt %s --canonicalize | FileCheck %s. Its expected iterator has one incoming slot, while the nested call still lists that slot twice. ↗ kernel_operands_basic.mlir:1 ↗ kernel_operands_basic.mlir:20

BEFORE · schematic, X:f32[2,3,4]

    inputs(%x as %a, %x as %b) outputs(%out) {
      map.call.opaque @kernels.add               // two mathematical call operands
        inputs(%a,%b) outputs(%out)

  mo.output %r                                  // same graph output

AFTER

  mo.output %r                                  // result computation unchanged

The native helper keys its seen map by Value. It replaces uses of each duplicate block argument, then removes duplicate operand slots in reverse order so later indices do not shift before they are processed:

for (unsigned idx : duplicates)
  rewriter.replaceAllUsesWith(inputArgs[idx], seen.lookup(getInputs()[idx]));
rewriter.modifyOpInPlace(getOperation(), [&] {
  for (unsigned idx : llvm::reverse(duplicates))
    eraseInputsAt(idx, 1);
});

Same shape, dtype or even equal numerical contents do not establish the SSA identity required by this map. ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:295 ↗ kernel_operands_basic.mlir:23

Captures are a second boundary. The file's @dedupes_prologue_captures starts with one opaque input but two captures of that same input inside a prologue. Its first load is dead; only the second feeds map.yield. The canonicalizer deduplicates captures and removes the unused load:

BEFORE · schematic prologue body
  prologue(index i) captures(c0=A,c1=A) {         // two captures of the same Value
    v0 = map.load c0[i]                          // unused scalar result
    v1 = map.load c1[i]                          // live scalar result
    map.yield v1                                // callback returns A[i]
  }

AFTER · canonicalizer fixed point
  prologue(index i) captures(c=A) {               // one capture slot and block argument
    v = map.load c[i]                            // surviving load
    map.yield v                                 // same returned scalar
  }

DedupeCapturingClosureCaptures performs the analogous Value-based replacement. DropDeadCapturingClosureCaptures then erases a capture if its shadowing argument has no uses. The test's CHECK-NEXT sequence requires one capture, one load and its yield; this is not a claim that deduplication itself performs arithmetic CSE. ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:40 ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:56 ↗ MAPCanonicalization.cpp:69 ↗ kernel_operands_basic.mlir:49

Example 7 · Why can a dtype-changing epilogue add a scratch result without adding a graph output?

TEST · MO → fusion → accumulation assignment. mixed-precision-matmul.mlir imports test kernels, runs --mo-to-map, --map-fuse-kernels, and --map-allocate-accumulating-buffers. Its @matmul_cast computes Matmul in f32 and casts the result to si32, all at shape [2,2]. The checks require two iterator outputs, si32 and f32, and an epilogue intermediate operand of f32. The graph continues to return only the cast result. RUN Input and expected scratch

BEFORE this pass · schematic, cast already fused
  %o = map.iter.opaque inputs(A:f32[2,2],B:f32[2,2])
    outputs(%oi:si32[2,2]) {                       // one external result destination
    %ep = epilogue(value m:f32,index i) captures(%oi) {
      n = map.call.elementwise Cast(i,m) : si32     // convert after producing m
      map.store %oi[i] = n                         // final store has integer dtype
    } intermediate=absent
    map.call.opaque Matmul inputs(A,B) outputs(%ep) // kernel still produces f32
  }
  mo.output %o                                    // one si32 graph result

AFTER
  %o,%scratch = map.iter.opaque inputs(A,B)
    outputs(%oi:si32[2,2],%tmp:f32[2,2]) {          // extra internal destination
    %ep = epilogue(value m:f32,index i)
      intermediate %tmp captures(%oi) {            // producer accumulation source is f32
      n = map.call.elementwise Cast(i,m) : si32     // same postprocessing
      map.store %oi[i] = n                         // final output stays si32
    }
    map.call.opaque Matmul inputs(A,B) outputs(%ep) // same f32 producer contract
  }
  mo.output %o                                    // scratch is not a new user output

findStoreTarget searches direct stores in the epilogue body and prefers a destination whose element type matches the incoming scalar. The assignment path creates scratch only when the chosen output type differs and containsMatmulOrConvOrConcat(kernel) identifies an accumulating kernel:

Type scratchType = resultTy.cloneWith(*inDType);
BlockArgument scratchArg;
IterOpaqueOp newKernel =
    addScratchResult(kernel, scratchType, scratchArg);
epi.getIntermediateTensorMutable().assign(scratchArg);
return assignIntermediateTensors(newKernel);

An operation's result list cannot grow in place. addScratchResult creates a replacement iterator, copies device/effects/dispatch/provenance, moves the old region with takeBody, appends a scratch output block argument, redirects old result users and erases the old iterator. The recursive assignment resumes on the replacement and skips the already assigned epilogue. Target selection Predicate and assignment Iterator replacement

For illustrative A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[5,6],[7,8]], the f32 products are [[19,22],[43,50]], and the final si32 values are the same integers. Both tensor types occupy four bytes per element here; scratch is needed to preserve the accumulation type, even though this test's two element widths happen to match. The added f32 [2,2] result describes 16 bytes of logical storage. This pass records that storage requirement in IR; it does not allocate a device address. Scratch type construction

Matched alternative, no extra scratch: @matmul_add_and_cast has two final destinations, one f32 and one si32, after horizontal/output fusion. findStoreTarget can use the existing f32 destination as intermediateTensor, so no third result is added. The sibling test reverses the store order and still expects the f32 destination: selection follows dtype, not the first store. Two-output expectation Reversed-order expectation

An already assigned intermediate is skipped, a same-dtype store normally becomes the intermediate directly, and an attention opaque with no epilogue has nothing to process. None of these branches introduces the attention score matrix or changes BN/BD. Skip and direct-target paths ↗ fused_attention.mojo:82

Example 8 · Why can a pure slice or reshape become a standalone view again before outlining?

TEST · the pass sees the output of MO→MAP. raise-back-contiguous-views.mlir supplies MO slice/reshape operations, imports built-ins, lowers them with --mo-to-map, then runs --map-raise-back-contiguous-views. The matched slice keeps complete trailing rows: [10,64] sliced by starts [1,0], stops [4,64], steps [1,1] gives [3,64]. CHECK-NOT excludes the former iterator and CHECK requires scalar bounds plus mogg.slice. RUN Contiguous input and expectation

BEFORE this pass · schematic, old bound constants omitted
  %s = map.iter.elementwise<[3,64]>                 // pure view iterator
    inputs(X,start,stop,step) outputs(S) index(i) {
      j = map.index.slice<starts=[1,0],stops=[4,64],steps=[1,1]>(i,start,stop,step)
                                                    // [r,c] → [r+1,c]
      v = map.load X[j]                             // the body's only load
      map.store S[i] = v                            // unchanged loaded value
    }
  mo.output %s                                     // shape [3,64]

AFTER
  %start0 = mo.constant 1 : si64[]                  // scalar first-row bound
  %stop0  = mo.constant 4 : si64[]                  // scalar exclusive stop
  %s = mogg.slice(X,%start0,%stop0) : f32[3,64]      // standalone contiguous slice view
  mo.output %s                                     // same selected rows

matchViewChain accepts only a body consisting of slice/reshape index transformations, one input load, and its output store. For a slice, matchContiguousSliceDim requires known dimensions, unchanged extents outside the first non-unit input dimension, static bounds on that dimension and step 1. A matched chain is visited in reverse because its index operations run from output coordinates back to input, while data views are built from input toward output. Pure-view matcher Contiguity checks

The slice branch creates scalar bounds and then the view operation:

cur = MOGG::SliceOp::create(builder, op.getLoc(), outType, cur, startK,
                            stopK)
          ->getResult(0);

After rebuilding the view chain, it redirects users and erases the iterator. For illustrative row-major X[r,c]=100*r+c, the output element [0,7] is X[1,7]=107. Its offset from the original input base is 1×64+7=71 elements. The slice begins 64 elements into X, so the view-relative offset is 7; 64+7=71 preserves the address. The offsets describe the zero-copy view contract, not a measured pointer. View construction Replacement

Reshape companion: the same test's [4,6] → [24] pure reshape is raised back to mo.static.reshape. The original MO operation was replaced by MO→MAP; this pass creates a new MO reshape with the same view contract. It does not restart the earlier MO pipeline. Reshape test Reshape construction

BEFORE · pure flatten, schematic
  %r = iterator<[24]> {                             // structured view of X:f32[4,6]
    j = map.index.reshape<[4,6]->[24]>(i)          // [k] → [k/6,k%6]
    v = map.load X[j]                               // preserve linear element k
    map.store R[i] = v                              // no arithmetic
  }
AFTER
  %r = mo.static.reshape(X) : f32[4,6] -> f32[24]   // same 24 elements in order

Skipped case: slicing [10,64] to [3,32] with starts [1,32] changes both dimensions, leaving gaps between selected row tails. The test expects it to remain an elementwise view iterator under this pass. Dynamic bounds and a broadcast are also kept. Additional arithmetic in the body fails the pure-view matcher. Being skipped here does not imply that a later general strided-view route must copy the data. Noncontiguous case Dynamic bounds Broadcast case

Example 9 · How does outlining move a scalar body into an opaque container while preserving its operations?

TEST · input already contains a structured MAP iterator. outline-structured-kernel-bodies.mlir runs only --map-outline-structured-kernel-bodies. It supplies a [256,256] Add iterator plus a declaration stub needed to verify its scalar call. The checks require an enclosing map.iter.opaque, a map.iter.elementwise.body, captures for X/Y/O, and the same two loads, Add and store in that body. RUN and declaration Input and expected body

BEFORE · schematic, use smaller X/Y:f32[2,3] for reading
  %r = map.iter.elementwise<[2,3]>                 // structured outer iterator
    inputs(%x as %a,%y as %b) outputs(%o) index(%i) {
      %av = map.load %a[%i]                        // original scalar operation 1
      %bv = map.load %b[%i]                        // original scalar operation 2
      %v = map.call.elementwise Add(%i,%av,%bv)    // original scalar operation 3
      map.store %o[%i] = %v                        // original scalar operation 4
    }
  mo.output %r                                    // graph result

AFTER
  %r2 = map.iter.opaque                           // new outer kernel container
    inputs(%x as %xi,%y as %yi) outputs(%oi) {
    map.iter.elementwise.body<[2,3]>               // new capturing closure shell
      index(%j) captures(%a=%xi,%b=%yi,%o=%oi) {
        %av = map.load %a[%j]                      // same operation, new index use
        %bv = map.load %b[%j]                      // same operation
        %v = map.call.elementwise Add(%j,%av,%bv)  // same scalar call
        map.store %o[%j] = %v                      // same final store
      }
    }
  mo.output %r2                                   // redirected outer result use

outline copies the old iterator's input/result types, chain, device, effects, dispatch and provenance into a new opaque operation. Its new body arguments become closure captures. IterElementwiseOp::createBodyClosure constructs IterElementwiseBodyOp; the reduction counterpart constructs IterRowwiseBodyOp. Container creation Elementwise closure factory Rowwise closure factory

The implementation moves the old region; it does not clone its scalar operations:

Region &region = body.getBody();
region.takeBody(loop->getRegion(0));
Block &movedBody = region.front();
BlockArgument newIndexArg =
    movedBody.insertArgument(0u, oldIndexArg.getType(), loc);
oldIndexArg.replaceAllUsesWith(newIndexArg);
movedBody.eraseArgument(movedBody.getNumArguments() - 1);

The old block argument order is [X,Y,O,index]; the closure needs [index,X,Y,O]. Inserting a new index argument at position 0 and replacing the old index's uses accomplishes that reordering. The data arguments move with the block and now correspond to explicit captures. The old outer iterator is erased after its result uses move to the new opaque result. Body transfer and index repair

For illustrative X[1,2]=4, Y[1,2]=5, the same two loads and Add still produce 9. The outer iterator count stays one; the number of ownership boundaries grows from one iterator body to an opaque body containing a capturing closure. An opaque container produced this way retains a visible elementwise body, while the attention container holds a registered map.call.opaque. Those two containers have different contents even though their outer operation name matches. Body creation ↗ MOToMAP.cpp:238

QnA 8 · What does “MAP fusion optimizes eligible access patterns while preserving the custom-op boundary” mean? Does MAP optimize the kernel, and was anything inside it optimized in previous steps?

MAP optimizes the computation and memory accesses represented in the graph. For this custom attention operation, it does not expand P1’s Mojo body into separate matmul, softmax and multiplication nodes. Those operations remain inside the registered implementation. See MOToMAP.cpp:135.

“Preserving the custom-op boundary” means retaining this structure:

What MAP sees:

Q ──┐
K ──┼──► one opaque attention call ──► O
V ──┘                 │
                      └── references P1's implementation

What is inside P1:

tiles of Q, K, V
       │
       ▼
   Q × Kᵀ
       │
       ▼
online softmax + accumulator updates
       │
       ▼
   probabilities × V
       │
       ▼
   output tile

The internal calculations are Mojo statements inside the kernel. They are not separate MAP producer/consumer nodes that MAP fusion can combine. See the attention implementation.

Does MAP optimize kernels at all? Yes—when their computation or supported fusion interface is available to MAP.

For example, consider this illustrative graph:

BEFORE:
X ──► matmul kernel ──► temporary T ──► multiply by 2 ──► Y

AFTER, if the kernel supports a fused output callback:
X ──► matmul kernel ──► callback: multiply each result by 2
                                      │
                                      ▼
                                write directly to Y

The callback is an epilogue: work performed as the kernel produces its output. Fusion can eliminate the separate intermediate tensor and elementwise operation. The matmul algorithm can remain intact while its output processing changes. MAP checks for an existing epilogue, an eligible elementwise consumer and other conditions before performing this fusion. See OutputFusion.cpp:125.

Your attention kernel declares ordinary InputTensor and OutputTensor arguments. MO→MAP passes these directly; it creates load/store callbacks only for arguments declared as fused tensor types. Consequently, this attention call does not provide those input/output fusion sites. MAP can still simplify surrounding accesses, views and redundant representation where applicable. See the kernel arguments, the callback decision and the MAP pipeline.

What happened to the kernel before MAP?

Earlier step What happened
Author writes the attention kernel Tiling and incremental online softmax are already implemented together inside P1. MAP did not discover this combination.
P1 package creation mojo precompile parses the package, prepares serializable compiler representation, runs checks and writes .mojoc bytecode. This is package preparation rather than final GPU machine-code generation.
MO graph passes Verify and simplify graph contracts, shapes, constants and visible operations. They do not rewrite the hidden attention loop body.
MO→MAP Represent the attention call and its input/output access contract in MAP.

These distinctions follow from the attention source, package creation and the MO pipeline.

Later, the Mojo compiler processes the actual implementation, specializing it for the call’s parameters and target and lowering it toward native code. The kernel JIT imports the library, runs elaboration on a cache miss and emits compiled code. Thus, the opaque boundary at MAP does not prevent later compilation and optimization of P1’s implementation. See JitCompileKernels.cpp:440.

QnA 9 · How does FuseKernelsPass::runOnOperation work? Explain its ordered elementwise, view, prologue, reduction, epilogue, reshape-epilogue and horizontal fusion passes, CSE cleanup and repeat loop with C++ code, diagrams and before/after compiler transformations.

FuseKernelsPass rewrites the compiler’s graph so eligible computations share an iteration body or a kernel callback. Below is the complete explanation with the relevant C++ code interleaved beside each transformation.

The numeric examples and MAP snippets are schematic. The C++ excerpts are selected lines from the implementation; ... indicates omitted surrounding code.

Start with the Add→Multiply example.

X = [ 1,  2,  3]
Y = [10, 20, 30]
Z = [ 2,  3,  4]

T = X + Y       # add corresponding elements
O = T * Z       # multiply corresponding elements

Here, Add is the producer because it produces T. Multiply is the consumer because it reads T.

BEFORE FUSION

X ──┐
    ├──► Add ──► T ──────┐
Y ──┘                    ├──► Multiply ──► O
                    Z ───┘

T = [11, 22, 33]
O = [22, 66, 132]

This matches the graph in basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:3, using a smaller tensor here.

“Elementwise” means each output position uses the corresponding input positions.

Index 0: (X[0] + Y[0]) * Z[0] = (1 + 10) * 2 =  22
Index 1: (X[1] + Y[1]) * Z[1] = (2 + 20) * 3 =  66
Index 2: (X[2] + Y[2]) * Z[2] = (3 + 30) * 4 = 132

Both calculations share index i. No transpose or reshape changes which input position they access. This is the case handled by the elementwise fuser. See ElementwiseFuser.cpp:14.

Before fusion, MAP represents two iteration bodies:

T = map.iter.elementwise over [3]:
      a = map.load X[i]
      b = map.load Y[i]
      t = Add(a,b)
      map.store T[i] = t

O = map.iter.elementwise over [3]:
      t = map.load T[i]
      c = map.load Z[i]
      o = Multiply(t,c)
      map.store O[i] = o

After fusion:

O = map.iter.elementwise over [3]:
      a = map.load X[i]
      b = map.load Y[i]
      t = Add(a,b)
      c = map.load Z[i]
      o = Multiply(t,c)
      map.store O[i] = o
AFTER FUSION

X ──┐
Y ──┼──► one fused iteration ──► O
Z ──┘
             │
             └── O[i] = (X[i] + Y[i]) * Z[i]

t remains a local intermediate value inside the body. The separate tensor T and the store/load through it are unnecessary. The test checks for one map.iter.elementwise containing both scalar calls and the final store. See basic_pointwise_fusion.mlir:13.

Now connect this to the complete pass.

FuseKernelsPass::runOnOperation()
│
├─ obtain the current mo.graph
│
├─ construct fusePm
│  └─ ordered fusion round:
│     ├─ FuseElementwise
│     ├─ FuseViews
│     ├─ FusePrologue
│     ├─ FuseReductions
│     ├─ FuseEpilogue
│     ├─ FuseReshapeEpilogue
│     └─ FuseHorizontal
│
├─ construct cleanupPm containing CSE
│
└─ repeat:
   ├─ count MAP iteration operations
   ├─ run the entire fusion round
   ├─ measure the decrease in count
   ├─ run CSE cleanup
   └─ continue if the count decreased

The implementation is in FuseKernels.cpp:37.

Obtain the current mo.graph.

MO::GraphOp graphOp = getOperation();

graphOp refers to the existing compiler IR graph being processed. Its body already contains MAP operations produced by MO→MAP. It does not construct another Python Graph object.

graphOp : mo.graph
└─ body
   ├─ inputs: X, Y, Z
   ├─ Add iteration       → T
   ├─ Multiply iteration  → O
   └─ mo.output O

The transformations operate inside this graph. See FuseKernels.cpp:38.

Construct the ordered pass manager.

mlir::OpPassManager fusePm(MO::GraphOp::getOperationName());

fusePm.addPass(createFuseElementwise());
fusePm.addPass(createFuseViews());
fusePm.addPass(createFusePrologue());
fusePm.addPass(createFuseReductions());
fusePm.addPass(createFuseEpilogue());
fusePm.addPass(createFuseReshapeEpilogue());
fusePm.addPass(createFuseHorizontal());

createFuseElementwise() constructs a compiler pass object. addPass(...) adds it to the manager. The graph is transformed later, when runPipeline(fusePm, graphOp) executes this list.

Each pass sees the graph as modified by preceding passes. A pass with no eligible pattern leaves it unchanged. See FuseKernels.cpp:46.

The following examples are separate comparison graphs. They do not imply that all seven passes modify our original Add→Multiply graph.

1. FuseElementwise: insert producer arithmetic into the consumer.

The pass selects elementwise bodies without view transformations:

config.shouldFuse = [](StoreOp srcStore, LoadOp dstLoad) {
  auto src = srcStore->getParentOfType<IterElementwiseOp>();
  auto dst = dstLoad->getParentOfType<IterElementwiseOp>();
  return src && dst && !isViewForeach(src) && !isViewForeach(dst);
};

...

numKernelsFused = fuseInput(getOperation(), config);

For Add→Multiply:

src = Add iteration
dst = Multiply iteration

srcStore = store T[i] = Add(X[i],Y[i])
dstLoad  = load T[i]

The predicate accepts this pair because both belong to elementwise iteration bodies without view index transformations. See ElementwiseFuser.cpp:64.

The shared spliceProducer implementation performs the rewrite:

dst.insertInputsAt(argIdx, src.getInputs());

...

rewriter.cloneRegionBefore(src.getBody(), dstRegion,
                           dstRegion.begin());

...

Value fusedVal = storeOp.getValue();
rewriter.eraseOp(storeOp);

...

fusedArgs.push_back(load.getIndex());
rewriter.inlineBlockBefore(&srcClone, load, fusedArgs);
rewriter.replaceOp(load, fusedVal);

For our example, these lines mean:

1. Multiply previously takes [T,Z].
   Add's inputs [X,Y] are introduced into Multiply's body.

2. Clone Add's body.

3. Remove the cloned store into T.
   Keep the value that Add would have stored: t = X[i]+Y[i].

4. Run that cloned body at Multiply's load index i.

5. Replace "load T[i]" with the computed value t.

See InputFusion.cpp:394.

Once the old Add result has no users, the shared driver removes the original producer:

if (src.getResult(0).use_empty()) {
  erased.insert(src);
  src->erase();
}

cast<IterOpInterface>(op).dedupeInputs(rewriter);

The resulting transformation is:

BEFORE:
  Add inputs      = [X,Y]
  Multiply inputs = [T,Z]

AFTER:
  fused inputs    = [X,Y,Z]
  fused body      = Add followed by Multiply
  result          = O
  old Add unit    = removed

See InputFusion.cpp:437.

2. FuseViews: insert the view’s index mapping into its consumer.

Consider transpose followed by addition:

X : shape [2,3]             B : shape [3,2]

    [1 2 3]                    [10 20]
    [4 5 6]                    [30 40]
                               [50 60]

T = transpose(X)           # T[i,j] reads X[j,i]
O = T + B                  # add corresponding elements
BEFORE:

X ──► Transpose ──► T ──┐
                       ├──► Add ──► O
                  B ───┘

T = [1 4]
    [2 5]
    [3 6]

The view fuser selects a producer whose stored value comes through a transformed load:

config.shouldFuse = [](StoreOp srcStore, LoadOp) {
  return producesThroughView(srcStore);
};

...

numKernelsFused = fuseInput(getOperation(), config);

See ViewFuser.cpp:35.

producesThroughView checks the producer’s dataflow for an index-transform operation:

return dataflowGraphContains<WalkDirection::Producers>(
    store.getValue().getDefiningOp(),
    [](Operation *o) {
      return isa<IndexTransformOpInterface>(o);
    });

In this example, the transpose index mapping qualifies. See InputFusion.cpp:43.

The same spliceProducer machinery moves that mapping and load into Add:

BEFORE, schematic MAP:

T iteration:
  inputIndex = transpose_index([i,j])   # produces [j,i]
  x = load X[inputIndex]
  store T[i,j] = x

O iteration:
  t = load T[i,j]
  b = load B[i,j]
  store O[i,j] = t+b
AFTER:

O iteration:
  inputIndex = transpose_index([i,j])
  x = load X[inputIndex]
  b = load B[i,j]
  store O[i,j] = x+b
X ──┐
    ├──► one iteration ──► O
B ──┘

O = [11 24]
    [32 45]
    [53 66]

The transpose is implemented by the input index mapping inside the consumer. A separate materialized T is unnecessary when this fusion qualifies. The shared implementation records this as view fusion. See InputFusion.cpp:184.

3. FusePrologue: put input arithmetic inside a kernel’s existing load callback.

A prologue supplies an input value when the kernel requests it.

A = [ 1,  2,  3]
B = [10, 20, 30]
indices = [2,0]

T = A+B                   # [11,22,33]
O = gather(T,indices)     # select T[2], then T[0]
                         # [33,11]
BEFORE:

A,B ──► Add ──► T ──► Gather ──► O
                          ▲
                       indices

The pass accepts a producer feeding an opaque kernel’s prologue:

config.shouldFuse = [](StoreOp srcStore, LoadOp dstLoad) {
  return srcStore->getParentOfType<IterElementwiseOp>() &&
         dstLoad->getParentOfType<IterOpaqueOp>();
};

config.canDuplicate = [](IterElementwiseOp) {
  return false;
};

numKernelsFused = fuseInput(getOperation(), config);

This pass requires an existing callback and does not duplicate a producer across multiple consumers. See PrologueFuser.cpp:37.

The shared implementation clones the producer into that callback, removes its intermediate store, and replaces the callback’s old load:

rewriter.cloneRegionBefore(src.getBody(), closure.getBody(),
                           closure.getBody().begin());

...

Value fusedVal = storeOp.getValue();
storeOp.erase();

...

fusedArgs.push_back(loadIndex);
rewriter.inlineBlockBefore(&srcClone, oldLoad, fusedArgs);

oldLoad.getResult().replaceAllUsesWith(fusedVal);
oldLoad.erase();

See InputFusion.cpp:207.

The compiler transformation is:

BEFORE CALLBACK:
  callback(k):
    return load T[k]

AFTER CALLBACK:
  callback(k):
    a = load A[k]
    b = load B[k]
    return Add(a,b)
AFTER:

A,B ──► input callback ──► Gather ──► O
                              ▲
                           indices

Request k=2 → 3+30 = 33
Request k=0 → 1+10 = 11

A and B replace T as captured inputs. The Add→Gather transformation is checked in prologue_fusion.mlir:3.

4. FuseReductions: insert work into the reduction body or after its row result.

A reduction combines multiple elements—for example, summing a row.

X : shape [2,3]
    [1 2 3]
    [4 5 6]

B : shape [2,1]
    [10]
    [20]

T = X*X                         # square each element
R = sum(T,axis=1,keepdims=True)  # one sum per row
O = R+B                         # add one bias per row
BEFORE:

X ──► Square ──► T ──► Row sum ──► R ──► Add B ──► O

T = [ 1  4  9]        R = [14]        O = [24]
    [16 25 36]            [77]            [97]

The pass collects rowwise operations and repeatedly looks for eligible producers and consumers:

while (IterElementwiseOp src = findProducer(dst)) {
  fuseProducer(dst, src, rewriter);
  rewriter.eraseOp(src);
  ++numKernelsFused;
  changed = true;
}

if (IterElementwiseOp consumer = findConsumer(dst)) {
  dst = fuseConsumer(dst, consumer, rewriter);
  ++numKernelsFused;
  changed = true;
}

Here, dst is the rowwise reduction. See ReductionFuser.cpp:298.

Producer fusion uses the same shared splice:

spliceProducer(dst, src, rewriter);
stampFusion(dst, src, /*isProducer=*/true);
IterOpInterface(dst).dedupeInputs(rewriter);

Thus:

BEFORE REDUCTION BODY:
  reduce over c:
    t = load T[r,c]
    yield t

AFTER PRODUCER FUSION:
  reduce over c:
    x = load X[r,c]
    square = Multiply(x,x)
    yield square

See ReductionFuser.cpp:93.

For consumer fusion, the implementation associates the consumer’s load with the scalar value produced by the reduction:

storedValues[arg] =
    perRowStore(dst, result.getResultNumber()).getValue();

...

mapping.map(load.getResult(), storedValues.lookup(arg));
continue;

This replaces a reload of R[r,0] with the reduction’s already available result. The consumer’s remaining operations are cloned into the rowwise body. See ReductionFuser.cpp:206.

AFTER: one rowwise computation

For each row r:
  acc = reduce_sum over columns c:
          X[r,c]*X[r,c]

  b = load B[r,0]
  result = Add(acc,b)
  store O[r,0] = result
Row 0: 1²+2²+3²+10 = 24
Row 1: 4²+5²+6²+20 = 97

The consumer must operate over the per-row result shape—here [2,1]. The implementation can remove the old reduction output when nothing else needs it. Producer and consumer examples are checked in producers.mlir:6 and consumers.mlir:7.

5. FuseEpilogue: use a kernel’s produced value directly in output arithmetic.

An epilogue processes a value as the kernel produces it.

A = [1 2]       W = [1 0]       B = [10 20]
    [3 4]           [0 1]           [30 40]

T = matmul(A,W)   # W is identity, so T=A
O = T+B          # elementwise bias addition
BEFORE:

A,W ──► Matmul ──► T ──┐
                       ├──► Add ──► O
                  B ───┘

The pass accepts an untransformed read of the producer’s output:

config.shouldFuse = [](StoreOp, LoadOp consumerLoad) {
  return consumerReadsUntransformed(consumerLoad);
};

numKernelsFused = fuseOutput(getOperation(), config);

See EpilogueFuser.cpp:35.

The shared output-fusion implementation reads the value that the producer’s epilogue would store:

auto epilogueStore = getUniqueStore(epilogueBody);
Value val = epilogueStore.getValue();

...

load.getResult().replaceAllUsesWith(val);
load.erase();

For this example:

Consumer previously:
  t = load T[i,j]
  b = load B[i,j]
  result = Add(t,b)

Consumer after substitution:
  b = load B[i,j]
  result = Add(val,b)

val = the value Matmul supplied to its epilogue

See OutputFusion.cpp:246.

The implementation adds the consumer’s other inputs as captures, moves its body into the epilogue, and rebuilds the final store:

epilogueOp.getCapturesMutable().append(dstInputArg);

...

epilogueStore.erase();
rewriter.inlineBlockBefore(&srcBody, &epilogueBody,
                           epilogueBody.end());

...

StoreOp::create(rewriter, storeLoc, cap,
                storeTransform, finalVal);
AFTER:

A,W ──► Matmul ──► output callback ──► O
                         ▲
                         B

callback(val,i,j):
  b = load B[i,j]
  store O[i,j] = Add(val,b)

O = [11 22]
    [33 44]

The Matmul body remains the producer implementation; the Add moves into its output callback. See OutputFusion.cpp:298 and the checked pattern in epilogue_fusion.mlir:3.

6. FuseReshapeEpilogue: move output arithmetic through a reshape by changing destination indexing.

Suppose a supported kernel produces:

C : shape [2,3]
    [1 2 3]
    [4 5 6]

R = reshape(C,[6])        # same ordered elements, expressed as a vector
B = [10,20,30,40,50,60]
O = R+B
BEFORE:

Producer ──► C[2,3] ──► Reshape ──► R[6] ──► Add B ──► O[6]

The pass specifically selects a consumer that reads through a reshape and performs additional work:

config.shouldFuse = [](StoreOp, LoadOp consumerLoad) {
  return consumerReadsThroughReshape(consumerLoad) &&
         !consumerIsPureReshape(consumerLoad);
};

fuseOutput(getOperation(), config);

A bare reshape is excluded by this predicate. See ReshapeEpilogueFuser.cpp:35.

Before fusion, the consumer maps its vector position back to the producer’s matrix position:

Consumer index k → producer index [k//3, k%3]

k=4 → [1,1] → C[1,1]

After fusion, the producer supplies a matrix position, so the store needs the inverse mapping:

Producer index [r,c] → destination index k=r*3+c

[1,1] → k=4

The implementation swaps the reshape signature and creates a store-side index transform:

ViewSignatureAttr origSig = reshape.getSpec().getSignature();

auto swappedSpec = ReshapeSpecAttr::get(
    ctx,
    ViewSignatureAttr::get(ctx,
                           origSig.getOut(),
                           origSig.getIn()));

storeTransform = ReshapeIndexOp::create(
    rewriter, storeLoc,
    IndexType::get(ctx, origSig.getOut().getRank()),
    swappedSpec, storeIdx);

See OutputFusion.cpp:274.

The consumer’s load of C is replaced with the produced value, and its loop index is replaced with the transformed store index:

load.getResult().replaceAllUsesWith(val);
load.erase();

...

srcBody.getArguments().back()
    .replaceAllUsesWith(storeTransform);

This produces:

AFTER:

Producer ──► reshaping output callback ──► O[6]

callback(val,r,c):
  k = r*3+c
  b = load B[k]
  store O[k] = Add(val,b)

O = [11,22,33,44,55,66]

The kernel still produces values using [2,3] coordinates, while the destination uses shape [6]. The shared implementation preserves the producer-facing epilogue shape where needed and retypes the destination path. See OutputFusion.cpp:351 and reshape_epilogue_fusion.mlir:12.

7. FuseHorizontal: combine sibling bodies into one operation with multiple results.

Here neither computation consumes the other’s result:

X = [ 1,  2,  3]
Y = [10, 20, 30]
Z = [ 2,  3,  4]

O1 = X+Y
O2 = X+Z
BEFORE:

         ┌──► Add Y ──► O1
X ───────┤
         └──► Add Z ──► O2

The fuser requires compatible shape and device, a shared loaded operand, and valid dependency/effect conditions. See HorizontalFuser.cpp:105.

Its construction combines inputs and result types:

SmallVector<Value> inputs(a.getInputs());

...

auto *it = llvm::find(inputs, in);
if (it == inputs.end())
  inputs.push_back(in);

...

SmallVector<Type> resultTypes(a->getResultTypes());
llvm::append_range(resultTypes, b->getResultTypes());

For our example:

a inputs = [X,Y]
b inputs = [X,Z]

combined inputs  = [X,Y,Z]
combined results = [O1,O2]

See HorizontalFuser.cpp:405.

The implementation creates the combined iterator, clones both bodies into it, and redirects uses of their results:

cloneBody(a, aSlots, 0, bodyBuilder, index);

...

cloneBody(b, slotForBInput, a->getNumResults(),
          bodyBuilder, index);

...

a.replaceAllUsesWith(fused.getResults().take_front(split));
b.replaceAllUsesWith(fused.getResults().drop_front(split));

b.erase();
a.erase();

Both bodies are mapped to the same iteration index. Users of O1 and O2 now use the respective results of the new operation. See HorizontalFuser.cpp:472.

AFTER:

X,Y,Z ──► one iteration ──┬──► O1
                         └──► O2

For each i:
  x = load X[i]
  y = load Y[i]
  z = load Z[i]

  store O1[i] = Add(x,y)
  store O2[i] = Add(x,z)

O1 = [11,22,33]
O2 = [ 3, 5, 7]

The isolated horizontal pass can initially leave duplicate loads of X; the CSE cleanup described next collapses equivalent loads. This distinction is documented in horizontal_fusion.mlir:3.

Why does the pass order matter?

Earlier passes can create a larger body that a later pass absorbs.

For example:

BEFORE:

A ──► Add A ──► Cast ──► Softmax
After FuseElementwise:

A ──► [Add + Cast] ──► Softmax
After FusePrologue:

A ──► Softmax
       └─ input callback:
            load A
            Add
            Cast
            supply the resulting value

The first pass combines the arithmetic body. The later prologue pass moves that whole body into Softmax’s existing input callback. The repository checks this chain in prologue_fusion.mlir:64.

Input/view fusion likewise runs before output fusion so a view and its consumer can become one body before that body moves into an epilogue. Horizontal fusion runs last, after these producer–consumer opportunities. This ordering rationale is documented in FuseKernels.cpp:40.

CSE cleanup: reuse equivalent computations.

CSE means Common Subexpression Elimination.

The cleanup manager contains the CSE pass:

mlir::OpPassManager cleanupPm(MO::GraphOp::getOperationName());
cleanupPm.addPass(mlir::createCSEPass());

See FuseKernels.cpp:60.

For the horizontally combined body:

Before CSE:
  x1 = load X[i]
  o1 = Add(x1,Y[i])

  x2 = load X[i]          # equivalent load
  o2 = Add(x2,Z[i])
After CSE:
  x = load X[i]
  o1 = Add(x,Y[i])
  o2 = Add(x,Z[i])

Where legal, both calculations reuse the same loaded value. The full fusion pass runs this cleanup after each round; it does not run a full canonicalization between rounds. See FuseKernels.cpp:57.

Count the computation units and repeat the round.

The counting function visits MAP iteration operations:

auto kernelCount = [&] {
  unsigned n = 0;
  graphOp.getBody().walk([&](IterOpInterface) {
    ++n;
    return WalkResult::skip();
  });
  return n;
};

WalkResult::skip() avoids descending further into a counted iteration operation. For example, the nested reduction inside a rowwise body is not counted as another independent outer computation unit by this walk. See FuseKernels.cpp:64.

The main loop is:

unsigned fused;
do {
  unsigned before = kernelCount();

  if (failed(runPipeline(fusePm, graphOp)))
    return signalPassFailure();

  fused = before - kernelCount();
  numKernelsFused += fused;

  if (failed(runPipeline(cleanupPm, graphOp)))
    return signalPassFailure();

} while (fused > 0);

This code:

  1. Counts the current computation units.
  2. Runs all seven fusion passes.
  3. Measures the decrease.
  4. Records it in the pass statistic.
  5. Runs CSE cleanup.
  6. Repeats if the count decreased.

If a nested pipeline fails, the pass reports failure rather than continuing. See FuseKernels.cpp:80.

For our isolated Add→Multiply example:

ROUND 1
├─ before = 2
├─ FuseElementwise: Add + Multiply become one iteration
├─ remaining passes: no further eligible pattern here
├─ after = 1
├─ fused = 2-1 = 1
└─ CSE cleanup; repeat

ROUND 2
├─ before = 1
├─ all seven passes: no further fusion here
├─ after = 1
├─ fused = 1-1 = 0
└─ CSE cleanup; stop

A later pass can expose an opportunity for an earlier pass, which motivates another complete round. The number of rounds depends on the graph; individual fusers can also drain a chain within one invocation. See FuseKernels.cpp:75 and InputFusion.cpp:462.

Not every adjacent pair qualifies. Operation kinds, index transformations, device compatibility, block boundaries, result uses and duplication rules determine eligibility. Our original example has one consumer of T, so it avoids the multiple-consumer duplication case. These checks are in ElementwiseFuser.cpp:64 and InputFusion.cpp:315.

#ifndef GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_MAPDIALECT_MAPTRANSFORMS_TD
#define GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_MAPDIALECT_MAPTRANSFORMS_TD

include "mlir/Pass/PassBase.td"

def FuseKernels : Pass<"map-fuse-kernels", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Fuse MAP kernels by inlining producers into consumers.";
  let description = [{
    Runs the advanced fusion patterns over the MAP dialect, reducing the number
    of `map` kernels by inlining producers into consumers.

    Anchored on `mo.graph` (which is `IsolatedFromAbove` and always a direct
    child of the module), so the pass never walks the imported kernel decls or
    the insides of kernels it already visited, and independent graphs run in
    parallel.

    Repeats epilogue, elementwise, view, then prologue fusion until a round
    fuses nothing, since folding one link of a chain can expose the next.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];

  let statistics = [
    Statistic<"numKernelsFused", "num-kernels-fused", "Number of kernels fused">
  ];
}

def FuseEpilogue : Pass<"map-fuse-epilogue", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Fuse MAP kernels via EpilogueFuser only. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs `EpilogueFuser` alone so a lit test can exercise it in isolation.
    Not part of `buildMapPipeline`.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];
}

def FuseHorizontal : Pass<"map-fuse-horizontal", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Fuse sibling MAP kernels that share an input.";
  let description = [{
    Merges two `map.iter.elementwise` ops over the same index space that share an
    input into one multi-output kernel, so the shared operand is loaded once
    rather than by each kernel. Pairs siblings, where the other fusers pair a
    producer with its consumer. Also moves a consumer into its producer's
    epilogue when the producer's result has other readers, which output
    fusion leaves alone; a consumer that reads a strided window of the result
    runs there under a `map.index.slice.select`.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];
}

def FuseReshapeEpilogue : Pass<"map-fuse-reshape-epilogue", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary =
      "Fuse MAP kernels via ReshapeEpilogueFuser only. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs `ReshapeEpilogueFuser` alone so a lit test can exercise it in
    isolation. Not part of `buildMapPipeline`.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];
}

def FuseElementwise : Pass<"map-fuse-elementwise", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Fuse MAP kernels via ElementwiseFuser only. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs `ElementwiseFuser` alone so a lit test can exercise it in isolation.
    Not part of `buildMapPipeline`.
  }];

  let options = [
    Option<"largeTensorElementThreshold", "large-tensor-element-threshold",
           "int64_t", /*default=*/"4096",
           "Tensor operands with more static elements than this (or with an "
           "unknown element count) are considered large; a kernel with more "
           "than one large tensor operand is not duplicated into multiple "
           "consumer subgraphs.">,
    Option<"maxFusionSetSize", "max-fusion-set-size", "uint64_t",
           /*default=*/"64",
           "Cap on the number of kernels fused into one consumer, bounding the "
           "duplication of a cheap multi-use producer across an elementwise "
           "chain with fan-out.">,
  ];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];
}

def FuseViews : Pass<"map-fuse-views", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Fuse MAP kernels via ViewFuser only. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs `ViewFuser` alone so a lit test can exercise it in isolation. Not
    part of `buildMapPipeline`.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];

  let statistics = [
    Statistic<"numKernelsFused", "num-kernels-fused", "Number of kernels fused">
  ];
}

def FusePrologue : Pass<"map-fuse-prologue", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Fuse MAP kernels via PrologueFuser only. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs `PrologueFuser` alone so a lit test can exercise it in isolation.
    Not part of `buildMapPipeline`.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];
}

def FuseReductions : Pass<"map-fuse-reductions", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Fuse MAP kernels into rowwise reductions. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs the reduction fuser alone. A producer only a `map.iter.rowwise`
    reads is cloned at each load of its result. A consumer over the per-row
    shape that reads a per-row result at its own index becomes row-level
    ops, and its result a rowwise output.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];

  let statistics = [
    Statistic<"numKernelsFused", "num-kernels-fused", "Number of kernels fused">
  ];
}

def FuseInput : Pass<"map-fuse-input", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Unconstrained generic input fusion. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs generic input fusion with no wrapper constraint: every eligible
    producer/consumer edge fuses, subject only to the shared correctness
    constraints. Not part of `buildMapPipeline`.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];
}

def FuseOutput : Pass<"map-fuse-output", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Unconstrained generic output fusion. For testing only.";
  let description = [{
    Runs generic output fusion with no wrapper constraint: every eligible
    epilogue edge fuses, subject only to the shared correctness constraints.
    Not part of `buildMapPipeline`.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];
}

def OutlineStructuredKernelBodies
    : Pass<"map-outline-structured-kernel-bodies", "mlir::ModuleOp"> {
  let summary =
      "Outline structured MAP kernel bodies into `map.iter.opaque` regions.";
  let description = [{
    Wraps each structured MAP loop (`map.iter.elementwise`, `map.iter.rowwise`) in
    a `map.iter.opaque` region so sequential setup (e.g. strided-view lifting)
    can live outside the structured loop body. The loop's own shape and body
    move into a nested `map.iter.elementwise.body` or `map.iter.rowwise.body`,
    which reaches the wrapper's inputs/outputs through its captures.
    After outlining, nothing inspects the inside of the `map.iter.opaque` again.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
  ];
}

def LoopInvariantViewMotion : Pass<"map-livm", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary =
      "Hoist chains of index-transform ops out of a structured loop body.";
  let description = [{
    Runs after `OutlineStructuredKernelBodies`, over every `map.iter.opaque`
    in the graph, including ones nested in control-flow regions. It anchors on
    `mo.graph` because a pass adaptor does not descend into an `mo.while`,
    `mo.if` or `mo.parallel` body. The rewrite is mandatory: an unhoisted
    index-transform op has no `LowerableToMOGGInterface` and strands
    `map-to-mogg`.

    For each `map.load` in a `map.iter.elementwise.body`, walks back from its index
    through any chain of `MAP::IndexTransformOpInterface` ops (today:
    `map.index.slice`) to the loop's own index, hoists each hop into a "stride"
    op (today: `map.index.slice.stride`) in the enclosing `map.iter.opaque`, so
    it runs once per kernel invocation rather than once per index, and rewrites
    the load to index the hoisted tensor with the untransformed index. Loads
    that hoist an SSA-identical chain share one hoisted op.

    Invariant: only index-transform ops that feed a store index survive.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
  ];
}

def RaiseBackContiguousViews
    : Pass<"map-raise-back-contiguous-views", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Raise unfused slice/reshape view kernels back to MO/MOGG ops.";
  let description = [{
    Runs after `FuseKernels`, before `OutlineStructuredKernelBodies`. Raises
    unfused `map.iter.elementwise` view kernels back into ops `MOGGToMGP` lowers
    without a copy: a contiguous slice becomes `mogg.slice`
    (`mgp.tensor.slice`), and a reshape becomes `mo.static.reshape`. Like
    `mogg-fuse-views`, only slice and reshape, not broadcast/transpose.
  }];

  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MO::MODialect",
    "M::MOGG::MOGGDialect",
  ];

  let statistics = [
    Statistic<"numSlicesRaised", "num-slices-raised",
              "Number of contiguous slice kernels raised back">,
    Statistic<"numReshapesRaised", "num-reshapes-raised",
              "Number of reshape kernels raised back">
  ];
}

def FuseMutableLoads : Pass<"map-fuse-mutable-loads", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "'Fuse' mo.mutable.load ops with map.iter.elementwise ops.";
  let description = [{
    Will perform 'fusion' of a mo.mutable.load op with a map.iter.elementwise op.
    This amounts to:
      1. Replacing the value semantic tensor created by the mutable.load op
         with the buffer semantic tensor
      2. Making the input chain of the load op an input of the
         map.iter.elementwise op
      3. Adding the output chain of the mutable.load op to the output of the
         map.iter.elementwise op
  }];
  let dependentDialects = ["M::MAP::MAPDialect"];
}

def AllocateAccumulatingBuffers
    : Pass<"map-allocate-accumulating-buffers", "MO::GraphOp"> {
  let summary = "Give every fused-output epilogue a real store pointer.";
  let description = [{
    Runs after `FuseKernels`. Sets each `map.iter.epilogue`'s
    `$intermediateTensor` so `MAPToMOGG` always has a real base pointer:

    - Normally the pointer source is the tensor the epilogue stores into.
    - For a mixed-precision accumulating kernel (`containsMatmulOrConvOrConcat`
      whose epilogue changes dtype), the kernel must accumulate in the pre-cast
      dtype before the lambda casts and stores. A fresh accumulation buffer of
      that dtype is allocated as an extra kernel output and used as the pointer
      source; the store target stays the real (post-cast) output.
  }];
  let dependentDialects = [
    "M::MAP::MAPDialect",
    "M::MO::MODialect",
  ];
}

#endif // GENERICML_GRAPHCOMPILER_MAPDIALECT_MAPTRANSFORMS_TD

#ifndef GENERICML_MO_GRAPHCOMPILER_PASSES_H
#define GENERICML_MO_GRAPHCOMPILER_PASSES_H

#include "AsyncRT/ForwardDecls.h"
#include "GraphCompiler/GraphCompiler.h"
#include "Support/AlignedAlloc.h"
